Empathize

Understanding the problem

EssentiallySports had scale — 30M+ monthly visitors — but the experience hadn't kept up. Dense layouts, cluttered navigation, and an outdated visual identity were creating friction at every turn.

Before
Before

The legacy homepage — competing elements, no clear hierarchy, weak content prioritization

Before
Before

ES ALL-STARS with broken image loading. Content sections with no visual or language hierarchy.

01
Overloaded Layouts
Too many competing elements at once — dense sections and inconsistent spacing raised cognitive load without raising engagement.
02
Poor Prioritization
Important stories didn't stand out. Users spent extra effort identifying what was worth clicking — language wasn't doing its job.
03
Fragmented Discovery
Content scattered across sections with no clear grouping. No strong directional flow while scrolling — users left instead of exploring.
04
Weak Visual Identity
The old wordmark and typography felt dated for a modern sports platform — hurting credibility, recall, and brand trust.
Define

Who are we designing for?

Research focused on behavioral analysis of sports news reading patterns. The central insight: users weren't lacking content — they were lacking clarity.

R
Rahul Mehta
The Daily Sports Scanner
Age: 26  ·  Occ: Lawyer
Habit: Scans during short breaks. Exits fast if confused.
"I just want to scan the big stories fast and move on."

Goals

  • Scan top stories instantly
  • Identify trending topics fast
  • No deep navigation needed
  • In and out in short sessions

Frustrations

  • Cluttered layouts slow scanning
  • Can't identify priority stories
  • Everything looks the same
  • Weak hierarchy — no clear path

User Journey Map

Mapped the full journey from homepage entry to exit — identifying exactly where engagement drops and where better design could create natural continuation loops.

Homepage → Article → Related Stories → Footer → Exit. Drop-off points mapped at each transition.

Ideate

Starting the design

Instead of jumping straight to hi-fi, I started with structural wireframes — establishing content hierarchy and reading flow before adding any visual treatment.

Exploration 01 — Hero Carousel
Primary Content Prioritization
The hero needed to do two things at once: surface the most important story instantly, and signal that more was available. Content labels like "ORIGINALS" and clear typographic hierarchy were the key decisions here.
  • Clear content labeling to signal story type
  • Controlled attention flow through layout hierarchy
  • Reduced competing elements around the primary story

Lo-fi carousel wireframe — "ORIGINALS" label, pagination dots, guided exploration

Exploration 02 — Homepage Layout
Business-Aware Content Structure
Newsletters are both an engagement and revenue channel at EssentiallySports. The redesigned layout gives newsletters clear prominence — improving discoverability without disrupting the reading flow.
  • Modular layout with clear section labels
  • Newsletter panel integrated — not an afterthought
  • Hierarchy that serves reader AND business goals

Homepage wireframe — primary story emphasis + newsletter panel side-by-side

Exploration 03 — Article Page
Continuation & Engagement Flow
Article pages had no strong post-read pathway. The wireframe introduced clear related stories placement and continuation cues — writing the next action directly into the layout.
  • Byline and author prominence for trust-building
  • "Related Stories" with intentional placement
  • Post-read engagement hooks built into layout

Article page wireframe — content hierarchy, byline placement, related stories zone

Prototype

High-fidelity explorations

Taking the wireframe structure into refined digital layouts — validating that content hierarchy and language decisions worked at full fidelity.

Prototype

Exclusives homepage — clean card grid, strong OLYMPICS + EXCLUSIVE labels, clear hierarchy

Prototype
Prototype

Left: NBA Week 18 + Our Newsletters panel — content and revenue side by side. Right: Originals carousel with strong editorial labeling.

Prototype

Article page — byline "Aayaan Sayadee," clear share actions, "Related Stories" continuation zone at bottom right

Test

Two rounds of refinement

Lightweight usability reviews across key surfaces. Round 1 surfaced friction. Round 2 validated the fixes.

Round 1 — Friction Found
1
Carousel intent wasn't clear
Users saw it as visual decoration, not interactive content. Labels needed to do more work.
2
Newsletter competed with content
Lacked sufficient separation — users couldn't distinguish editorial from subscription.
3
No post-read pathway
End of article had no clear next action. Sessions ended where they should have continued.
Round 2 — Validated
1
Clearer hierarchy improved scanning
Refined labels and modular grouping let users instantly identify primary vs secondary zones.
2
Engagement pathways felt natural
Better placement of related stories created natural post-read navigation loops.
3
Newsletter felt integrated
Clearer labeling made newsletter sections feel helpful rather than promotional.

Before vs. After

Structure, hierarchy, and language working together — the result is a platform where users know exactly where to look and what to do next.

Before
After

Clear zones. Strong labels. Intentional hierarchy. Users know exactly where to look.

Visual Identity

The old wordmark undercut the editorial authority the platform was building. Stronger typography, cleaner wordmark — the brand voice expressed visually.

→

A stronger wordmark reinforces trust and editorial authority — the same principles that guide good UX writing.

The Final Product

"Our Creators" — reels-style cards with strong brand identity, creator handles, and clear content labeling

Footer redesign — clear brand block, organized newsletter/sports/podcast columns, updated copyright

What I Bring

Three principles. Every project.

01
Journeys, not screens
I design how users move end-to-end. Structure, hierarchy, and flow working together — not individual screens in isolation.
02
Clarity with emotion
I balance usability with storytelling. Interfaces that are both readable and felt — especially in editorial and content-rich environments.
03
Iterate until it's right
I treat design as an evolving craft — shaped by reflection, testing, and the willingness to throw out what isn't working.
